doc.title: Tommy Newsom and Ross Tompkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

title: Head arrangements: Fletcher Henderson, Goodman and Herman
summary: Teddy Wilson and Neal Hefti told Tommy that classic tunes grew from head arrangements.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah. Oddly enough, I don’t think only that, I had a long conversation with Teddy Wilson one night, flying across the Atlantic believe it or not. And he was telling me about the old Fletcher Henderson band. This is slightly off the subject. But he went down this list of tunes, we got to talking about head arrangements. And all those things, like “King Porter Stomp” and “Big John Special”—
I remember “Big John Special.” “King Porter Stomp” is pretty complicated to be a head arrangement.
But it was. It just developed over time.
You know, the bass line and everything, how that goes.
Yeah. Well I mean there were parts—

But he said all those great old things that have come up, were things that guys in the band made up — “Sing Sing Sing” of Benny Goodman’s was mainly head I was told. Some of it was written out but they added things. And then I later talked to Neal Hefti a lot about the great Woody Herman band that made “Apple Honey” and “Caledonia” and all those things. And those things were head arrangements.
